1-1.text: Part one. Complete circuits. ... A simple circuit needs a cell to push the current, wires to carry it, and a component such as a bulb.

1-2.text: In circuit diagrams we draw symbols. Here are the symbols for a cell, a bulb, a switch and a wire. The long line of the cell is its positive side.

1-3.text: Current can only flow round a complete loop with no gaps. The switch is closed, so the bulb lights up.

1-4.text: Open the switch and you make a gap. The circuit is broken, so no current flows and the bulb goes out.

1-5.text: Current flows easily through conductors, like copper and other metals. Insulators, like plastic and rubber, stop it. That's why wires are covered in plastic.

2-1.text: Part two. Current. ... Current is a flow of electric charge round the circuit. A bigger current makes the same bulb glow more brightly.

2-2.text: We measure current in amps, with an ammeter. Its symbol is a circle with the letter A inside.

2-3.text: An ammeter goes in series: right in the loop, so all the current flows through it. This one reads nought point two amps.

2-4.text: We say current flows out of the positive side of the cell (the long line), round the circuit, and back into the negative side (the short line).

2-5.text: In a metal wire, the charges that really move are tiny electrons. They are negative, so they drift the other way: from negative to positive.

3-1.text: Part three. Potential difference. ... The cell gives the charges a push, and they carry energy to the bulb. The size of this push is the potential difference, also called the voltage.

3-2.text: Potential difference is measured in volts, with a voltmeter. Its symbol is a circle with the letter V inside.

3-3.text: A voltmeter is connected in parallel: across the bulb, with one wire on each side of it.

3-4.text: One cell gives about 1.5 volts. Two cells joined in a line give 3 volts. The bigger push makes a bigger current, so the bulb is brighter.

4-1.text: Part four. Series circuits. ... In a series circuit, everything is joined in one loop. There is only one path for the current.

4-2.text: The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Every ammeter here reads nought point two amps.

4-3.text: The potential difference is shared between the bulbs. Two cells give 3 volts, so two identical bulbs get 1.5 volts each.

4-4.text: Add another bulb in series and the current gets smaller, so every bulb is dimmer.

4-5.text: If one bulb breaks, it leaves a gap in the only path. The current stops and all the bulbs go out.

5-1.text: Part five. Parallel circuits. ... In a parallel circuit, the current splits into separate branches. Each bulb has its own loop back to the cell.

5-2.text: The currents in the branches add up to the current from the cell. These bulbs are identical: nought point three amps plus nought point three amps equals nought point six amps.

5-3.text: If one bulb breaks, the other branch is still a complete loop, so the other bulb stays on.

5-4.text: That's why the lights in a house are wired in parallel. Each light has its own switch, so one can be off while the others stay on.

6-1.text: Part six. Resistance. ... Resistance tells you how hard it is for current to flow through something. A resistor adds resistance. Its symbol is a rectangle.

6-2.text: Resistance is measured in ohms. With the same cells, more resistance means less current.

6-3.text: To work out resistance: resistance equals potential difference divided by current, or R equals V divided by I.

6-4.text: This resistor has 6 volts across it and 2 amps through it. R equals 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms.

6-5.text: You can turn it round to find the potential difference: V equals I times R. A current of 4 amps through 3 ohms needs 4 times 3, which is 12 volts.
